title: A tour of the 9 key governor races
contentHtml:
If you’re an avid Model Talk reader, you won’t be surprised by today’s newsletter. After taking tours through the most competitive House and Senate contests over the past two weeks, we’re moving on to the final class of races FLIPR forecasts: governors.

Gubernatorial elections can be less exciting for a national audience than federal races. (This article will probably receive less patronage than our Senate and House tours 😿). You might care about every Senate race because control of the chamber matters, but if you live in New York, your life is pretty much unaffected by whoever Kansas elects as governor. (Except — importantly — to the extent that governors play a role in Congressional redistricting.)

Indeed, some 2026 election forecasts don’t include gubernatorial races at all. But frankly, they can be harder to forecast. In governor races, fundraising information is less reliable1 and polling can be sparser. And some gubernatorial races are just plain weird, with ranked-choice voting like in Alaska or crazy primaries like for Democrats in Wisconsin. In these races, different assumptions might produce a different forecast, which is why today’s newsletter has a lot of Model Talk-type content.

The most important difference is that partisanship tells you far less in gubernatorial races: Vermont has a Republican governor, who is very likely to be re-elected, while Kentucky has a Democratic one. Since partisanship is part of the core of how FLIPR works, it therefore tends to treat gubernatorial races as more uncertain without the crutch of “Kentucky always votes for Republicans”, deferring to polls and expert ratings more than “fundamentals.”

All of this, by the way, reflects rational behavior from voters. Senate elections affect who controls the upper chamber of Congress. A Republican voter might like the Democratic Senate nominee. Maybe, deep down, they like him more than their own party’s nominee that year. But in an era of extreme party unity, electing him would put the Democrats one seat closer to a Senate majority. There are exceptions to this rule — Susan Collins, for example, has been repeatedly reelected in a state that is heavily Democratic at the presidential level — but they’re getting rarer and rarer.

Still, your state’s governor probably has more of an impact on your day-to-day life than your two senators. Once the majority has been decided in Congress, you’re electing people to a notoriously slow national body where members are increasingly likely to consistently vote the party line. Whereas a new governor can make sweeping changes to how a state is run relatively quickly.

At the moment, Republicans hold 26 governorships to Democrats’ 24, but Democrats govern more Americans than Republicans: approximately 194 million versus 146 million. That’s largely a function of Democrats controlling many of the largest states, such as California, New York, Illinois, and Pennsylvania.2 We like looking at things this way because unlike in the Senate, being the governor of Texas or California really is more important than being the governor of North Dakota — no offense, North Dakota.

FLIPR thinks Democrats are overwhelmingly likely to continue governing the most Americans after the midterms. In fact, they’re projected to govern 215 million compared to Republicans’ 127 million. Democrats also have a 62 percent chance of controlling the majority of governorships after November3, netting two seats in an average FLIPR simulation.

For this article, we’re going to focus on the seven gubernatorial elections where one party has at least a 25 percent chance of flipping the seat, plus two honorable mentions that fall just below that threshold. We’d note two important states that didn’t even make the list: Pennsylvania, where Josh Shapiro is an overwhelming favorite for re-election, and Michigan, where Jocelyn Benson is in a much safer position than Abdul El-Sayed and FLIPR rates the race as “Likely D”.

So instead we’ll start with the likeliest gubernatorial flip in the country, Iowa.

Iowa: Democratic flip probability 84 percent

Iowa’s current Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, isn’t seeking reelection. The state last elected a Democratic governor all the way back in 2006, although Barack Obama carried the state in 2008 and 2012.4 Still, it might seem like this year’s Republican nominee, Zach Lahn, should have a relatively smooth path to victory. Even though FLIPR estimates that Democrats will win the national popular vote by 6.6 points, Iowa is now red enough that its estimate of Iowa’s “simple fundamentals” — meaning the national generic ballot plus the state’s partisan lean — is R +3.

But maybe when Ann Selzer showed Kamala Harris ahead in Iowa by 3 points in 2024, she somehow traveled through time and polled the 2026 gubernatorial race instead. Because as of today, Iowa Auditor of State and Democratic candidate Rob Sand leads by about 5 points in our polling average. In fact, Sand has led in every one of the six Iowa gubernatorial polls in our database.
